answer.rationale: The binding constraints are the 14-day expiry and 94% line loading with no buffer. That combination effectively rules out switch_primary_vendor this cycle: memory_c2's cost win came from an onboarding that was 'quick' under unstated conditions, and a primary migration executed inside 14 days against a fully loaded line converts a cost objective into a delivery-risk objective. Similarly, defer_decision (memory_c5) is inapplicable because that record concerns a non-critical service that continued month-to-month; this contract does not auto-renew, so deferral is a supply lapse, not flexibility. add_second_source (memory_c3) is directionally sound but does not answer the expiring primary, and I only have one decision. Straight renew_incumbent (memory_c1) protects continuity but concedes the 18% mandate outright. That leaves negotiating the renewal. The incumbent has refused to reopen price 'this cycle', which is narrower than refusing all economic movement: memory_c4 shows benchmarking moved them on price and payment terms, and memory_c6 shows a longer commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope. A multi-year structure is therefore the live path to cost reduction that does not touch price-in-cycle, and it preserves the stable integration rather than gambling the line. I verify memory_c6 because it is the load-bearing assumption of this plan and the one whose failure would most change my action: if the archived record shows the multi-year volume pricing applied to a different, unconstrained category, or came with a commitment floor, or in fact did narrow scope, then multi-year is not a cost lever here and I would fall back to a short bridge renewal plus benchmarking pressure and revisit dual-sourcing next review. Risk I am explicitly carrying forward: a multi-year commitment made under a one-year cost mandate trades future optionality and negotiating leverage for present savings, and locks volume to a vendor who has just demonstrated it will refuse to reopen price. I would cap term length and require a benchmarking or volume-flex clause rather than accept lock-in as the price of the discount. I also do not treat the 18% target as certainly reachable through terms alone; if the negotiation lands short, the gap should be reported as a gap rather than closed by an unbudgeted migration.
